summary: Defines an RTP payload format for forward error correction using a 1-D interleaved parity code. Repair packets are sent in a separate flow from the source media, so a receiver can rebuild some lost packets.

eli5.summary: It is like sending a few extra puzzle hints with a message. If a piece goes missing, you can rebuild it from the hints without asking for it again.

questions: what is rtp forward error correction
how does xor fec recover lost packets
subtitle: A way to send XOR repair packets alongside RTP media so a receiver can rebuild packets lost in a burst.

tldr.problem: Real-time media over RTP suffers from bursty packet loss, and asking for retransmission may not be practical.
tldr.mechanism: The sender XORs groups of source packets that are L apart to make repair packets, with a 16-octet FEC header, and sends them in a separate repair flow. A receiver can rebuild one missing packet per group.
tldr.outcome: It gives good protection against bursts at reasonable complexity, but it is meant only for legacy uses such as DVB-IPTV, and newer fully RTP-compliant formats should be used where possible.

today: RFC 6015 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its own text says it should be used only in legacy applications, and that a fully RTP-compliant format such as RFC 5109 or a newer one must be used whenever possible.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
This RFC defines an RTP payload format for Forward Error Correction (FEC) generated by a 1-D interleaved parity code. It extends the FEC header of RFC 2733 and carries repair data for audio, video, text or application media sent over RTP (RFC 3550).

The code is systematic: source packets travel unchanged, and repair packets travel in a separate repair flow. The sender picks a set of source packets, XORs their symbols to make repair symbols, packetizes them and sends them with the source packets, either proactively or on demand. If nothing is lost, the receiver discards the repair packets.

Section 1.4 limits the scope: the format must only be used in legacy applications where the known limitations are harmless. Whenever possible, a fully RTP-compliant format such as RFC 5109 or a newer one must be used.
sections.eli5: The sender mails extra hint packets next to the real ones. If a real one gets lost, the hints can rebuild it, and if nothing is lost the hints are thrown away.

sections.title: The 1-D Interleaved Parity Code
sections.content:
Picture a source block of D rows and L columns, numbered from 1 to D x L. XORing the packets whose sequence numbers are L apart gives L repair packets, called interleaved or column FEC packets. Each repair packet protects D non-consecutive source packets.

A repair packet fully recovers the missing information only if exactly one packet is missing from its column. So the code handles bursts well, provided L is large enough: the duration of L packets should not be shorter than the burst to be repaired. If two or more random losses hit the same column, including its repair packet, recovery fails. Two bursts in the same source block can also defeat it.

The overhead is the ratio of repair bytes to protected source bytes. Assuming equal packet sizes and ignoring the FEC header, it is 1/D.
sections.eli5: Imagine packets in rows and each column gets one hint. If a whole row of neighbors is lost, each column is missing only one piece, so every column can fix itself.

sections.title: Relation to RFC 2733, SMPTE 2022-1 and DVB
sections.content:
This format is not backward compatible with the one registered by RFC 3009. It adopts the extended FEC header of SMPTE 2022-1, which replaces the bitmap with fields for the number of rows and columns and the repair packet type. It fixes parts of SMPTE 2022-1 that do not comply with RTP: that specification sets the SSRC to zero, ignores the repair timestamp and forbids CSRC entries.

One known issue stays for legacy reasons. The P bit, X bit and CC field of the repair packet's RTP header protect those fields of the source packets, which can fail RTP header validity checks. RFC 5109 fixed this, but this format keeps it.

The DVB-IPTV Application-layer FEC specification uses a base layer built from this interleaved parity code, which is mandatory wherever AL-FEC is used, and an optional Raptor enhancement layer.
sections.eli5: This builds on older recipes for packet hints used by video broadcasters. It cleans up some of the parts that did not follow the rules, but keeps one old quirk.

sections.title: Source and Repair Packets
sections.content:
Source packets are not modified. Their RTP sequence numbers already identify them, and leaving them alone keeps non-FEC receivers working in a multicast session.

A repair packet has an RTP header, a 16-octet FEC header and repair symbols. In the RTP header, the P, X, CC and M bits are the XOR sums of the same fields in the protected source packets, though padding, a header extension and a CSRC list are never actually present. The payload type is set out of band, so a receiver that does not know it discards the packet. The sequence number MUST be one higher than the previous repair packet's and starts at a random value. The timestamp SHALL match the repair packet's transmission time. The SSRC SHALL be randomly assigned, which lets source and repair flows share a port, and repair flows SHOULD use the RTCP CNAME to associate with the source flow.
sections.eli5: The real packets are sent as usual, so receivers without the hint feature still work. Hint packets have their own label, so those receivers just toss them out.

sections.title: The FEC Header
sections.content:
The FEC header uses these fields. SN base low is the lowest sequence number among the protected packets, with wraparound. Length recovery, PT recovery and TS recovery let a receiver rebuild the length, payload type and timestamp of a lost packet. Offset holds the number of columns (L) and NA the number of rows (D).

The E bit MUST be 1 to extend the RFC 2733 header. Mask, N, D, Index and SN base ext are set to 0 and ignored by the receiver, and Type MUST be 0 because only one code is defined. The RFC notes that a mask-based approach would become prohibitively large for big source blocks, so the systematized L and D approach is more efficient.
sections.eli5: The hint label says where the group starts, how wide and how tall it is, and a few facts needed to rebuild a missing packet, like its size and type.

sections.title: Media Types and SDP Parameters
sections.content:
The RFC registers 1d-interleaved-parityfec under four media types: audio, video, text and application. Each has the same required parameters: rate, the RTP clock rate in Hz (it SHALL be larger than 1000 and should match the source stream), L and D (positive integers up to 255), and repair-window, the time spanned by the FEC block in microseconds. A decoder SHOULD NOT report a decoding failure before waiting at least the repair window.

In SDP, the media type goes on the m= line, the subtype and rate on a=rtpmap, and the other parameters on a=fmtp. In offer/answer, each L and D combination yields different FEC data, and L and D set the lower limit of the repair window. Unknown options MUST be ignored. In declarative use, participants MUST use the configuration given.
sections.eli5: Before the call starts, both sides agree on the grid size and how long to wait for hints, using a short settings note.

sections.title: Building Repair Packets and Recovering Lost Ones
sections.content:
To build a repair packet, form a bit string for each protected source packet: the P, X, CC, M, PT, timestamp, and the length minus 12, followed by the CSRC list, extension, payload and padding. Shorter packets MUST be padded with zero octets to the longest length. XOR the bit strings; the result fills the repair packet's RTP header bits, PT recovery, TS recovery, Length recovery and the payload. Because of padding and the FEC header, a repair packet is larger than the packets it protects, which may exceed the path MTU.

To find which source packets a repair packet protects, compute SN base low + i x L (modulo 65536) for 0 <= i < D. If exactly one is missing, XOR the received source bit strings with the repair bit string to recover the RTP header and payload. The recovered packet gets version 2, the known sequence number and the SSRC of the source stream. Other algorithms are allowed, but the end result MUST be identical.
sections.eli5: To rebuild a lost piece, combine all the pieces you still have with the hint. What is left over is exactly the missing piece.

sections.title: Congestion and Security Considerations
sections.content:
FEC adds traffic. Where congestion causes the loss, applications MUST NOT arbitrarily increase FEC protection since that may lead to congestion collapse. Stronger protection MAY be applied only after the source rate is reduced, and protection is RECOMMENDED to adapt to the observed loss rate. In multicast, a sender may offer several repair flows with different protection levels.

On security, altering FEC packets can badly affect recovery. For example, changing the length recovery field can yield a packet that is too long, so sanity checks are helpful. If source packets are encrypted after FEC is applied, the FEC packets should be as secure as the source packets, or confidentiality, integrity or authentication can be compromised. SRTP is RECOMMENDED where suitable; IPsec and TLS are alternatives.
sections.eli5: Sending too many hints on a crowded road makes the traffic worse. And a bad hint can trick you into rebuilding a wrong piece.
